title: Inorganic Chemistry II
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 200L inorganic chemistry curriculum, second semester: transition metals and coordination chemistry (crystal field theory, ligands, complex nomenclature), acid-base theories (Arrhenius, Bronsted-Lowry, Lewis), the chemistry of Groups 16-18, and an introduction to nuclear chemistry/radioactivity. Deliberately distinct from CHM203's atomic structure/bonding/s-block/early p-block coverage.

questions.question: What is the defining electronic feature of transition metals, according to the IUPAC definition?
options: An incomplete d subshell in the atom or in at least one of its common ions
A completely full outer s subshell only
The absence of any d electrons
A completely empty valence shell
questions.correct_answer: An incomplete d subshell in the atom or in at least one of its common ions
questions.explanation: IUPAC defines a transition element as one whose atom (or at least one of its cations) has a partially filled d subshell, which gives rise to characteristic properties like variable oxidation states and coloured compounds.

questions.question: Which property is characteristic of many transition metal compounds but not typical of main group element compounds?
options: They are often brightly coloured due to d-d electron transitions
They never form ionic compounds
They cannot act as catalysts
They have no variable oxidation states
questions.correct_answer: They are often brightly coloured due to d-d electron transitions
questions.explanation: Partially filled d orbitals allow electrons to absorb visible light and transition between d energy levels split by ligand fields, producing the characteristic colours of many transition metal complexes.

questions.question: In the complex ion [Cu(NH3)4]2+, what is the coordination number of the central copper ion?
questions.explanation: The coordination number is the number of donor atoms directly bonded to the central metal ion; here, four ammonia ligands each donate one lone pair, giving a coordination number of 4.

questions.question: What is a ligand in coordination chemistry?
options: A molecule or ion that donates a lone pair of electrons to a central metal ion to form a coordinate bond
A metal ion that accepts electron pairs from other metal ions
Any anion present in a coordination compound's outer sphere only
A type of crystal lattice defect
questions.correct_answer: A molecule or ion that donates a lone pair of electrons to a central metal ion to form a coordinate bond
questions.explanation: Ligands act as Lewis bases, donating an electron pair to the central metal ion (a Lewis acid) to form the coordinate (dative) bonds that hold a coordination complex together.

questions.question: EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) is described as a hexadentate ligand. What does 'hexadentate' mean?
options: It can form up to six coordinate bonds to a single metal ion using six donor atoms
It can only bond to six different metal ions at once
It has six negative charges permanently
It reacts with exactly six water molecules
questions.correct_answer: It can form up to six coordinate bonds to a single metal ion using six donor atoms
questions.explanation: EDTA has six donor atoms (four oxygen and two nitrogen) that can simultaneously coordinate to one metal ion, making it hexadentate and forming very stable chelate complexes.

questions.question: According to crystal field theory, when ligands approach a transition metal ion, what happens to the previously degenerate d orbitals?
options: They split into sets of different energy levels due to differing electrostatic repulsion from the ligands
They merge into a single orbital of much lower energy
They disappear completely, leaving no d electrons
They remain exactly degenerate regardless of ligand type
questions.correct_answer: They split into sets of different energy levels due to differing electrostatic repulsion from the ligands
questions.explanation: Crystal field theory explains that approaching ligands create an electric field that affects the five d orbitals unequally depending on their orientation, splitting them into higher and lower energy sets (e.g., t2g and eg in octahedral complexes).

questions.question: In an octahedral complex, the d orbitals split into two sets. What are these two sets commonly called?
options: t2g and eg
sp3 and sp3d2
alpha and beta
bonding and antibonding only
questions.correct_answer: t2g and eg
questions.explanation: In octahedral crystal field splitting, the lower energy set of three orbitals is called t2g, and the higher energy set of two orbitals is called eg, with an energy gap known as the crystal field splitting energy, Delta(o).

questions.question: What is the correct IUPAC name for the complex ion [Fe(CN)6]4-?
options: Hexacyanoferrate(II) ion
Hexacyanoiron(IV) ion
Ferrate hexacyanide(II)
Iron hexacyanide(VI) ion
questions.correct_answer: Hexacyanoferrate(II) ion
questions.explanation: Ligands are named alphabetically with prefixes before the metal, the metal name uses the Latin root 'ferrate' with an '-ate' suffix because the complex is an anion, and the oxidation state of iron is +2 (since six CN- give -6 total charge, and overall charge is -4, iron must be +2).

questions.question: Which theory of acids and bases defines an acid as a substance that donates a proton (H+) and a base as a substance that accepts a proton?
options: Bronsted-Lowry theory
Arrhenius theory
Lewis theory
Kinetic theory
questions.correct_answer: Bronsted-Lowry theory
questions.explanation: The Bronsted-Lowry theory defines acids as proton donors and bases as proton acceptors, broadening the Arrhenius definition to include reactions not occurring in aqueous solution.

questions.question: According to the Lewis theory of acids and bases, how is a Lewis acid defined?
options: A substance that accepts a pair of electrons
A substance that donates a pair of electrons
A substance that releases hydroxide ions in water
A substance that donates a proton
questions.correct_answer: A substance that accepts a pair of electrons
questions.explanation: The Lewis theory, the broadest of the acid-base theories, defines a Lewis acid as an electron pair acceptor and a Lewis base as an electron pair donor, which is why metal ions acting as electron pair acceptors in coordination complexes are considered Lewis acids.

questions.question: In the Bronsted-Lowry reaction NH3 + H2O <-> NH4+ + OH-, which species is the conjugate acid of ammonia?
options: NH4+
H2O
OH-
NH3 itself
questions.correct_answer: NH4+
questions.explanation: The conjugate acid of a base is formed when the base accepts a proton; ammonia (NH3) accepts a proton to become NH4+, its conjugate acid.

questions.question: Why does the Arrhenius theory of acids and bases have limited applicability compared to the Bronsted-Lowry and Lewis theories?
options: It only applies to reactions occurring in aqueous solution
It cannot explain any acid-base reaction at all
It only applies to gases
It defines all substances as acids regardless of their behaviour
questions.correct_answer: It only applies to reactions occurring in aqueous solution
questions.explanation: Arrhenius defined acids as substances that increase H+ concentration and bases as those that increase OH- concentration specifically in water, so it cannot describe acid-base behaviour in non-aqueous or gas-phase systems, unlike the broader Bronsted-Lowry and Lewis theories.

questions.question: Which Group 17 element (halogen) exists as a diatomic gas at room temperature and is used as a disinfectant for water treatment?
options: Chlorine
Iodine
Astatine
Bromine
questions.correct_answer: Chlorine
questions.explanation: Chlorine (Cl2) is a pale yellow-green diatomic gas at room temperature widely used to disinfect drinking water and swimming pools due to its strong oxidizing and germicidal properties.

questions.question: How does the oxidizing power of the halogens change going down Group 17, from fluorine to iodine?
options: Oxidizing power decreases down the group
Oxidizing power increases down the group
Oxidizing power remains exactly constant
Only fluorine and chlorine have any oxidizing power
questions.correct_answer: Oxidizing power decreases down the group
questions.explanation: As atomic size increases and electron affinity weakens down the group, the ability of the halogen to gain an electron and act as an oxidizing agent decreases, making fluorine the strongest oxidizer and iodine the weakest.

questions.question: Chlorine gas can displace bromine from a solution of potassium bromide. What does this observation demonstrate?
options: Chlorine is a stronger oxidizing agent than bromine
Bromine is a stronger oxidizing agent than chlorine
Chlorine and bromine do not react with each other at all
Potassium bromide is insoluble in water
questions.correct_answer: Chlorine is a stronger oxidizing agent than bromine
questions.explanation: In this displacement reaction, Cl2 + 2KBr -> 2KCl + Br2, chlorine oxidizes bromide ions to bromine while itself being reduced, showing that chlorine is the stronger oxidizing agent, consistent with the trend of decreasing oxidizing power down Group 17.

questions.question: Which allotrope of oxygen, O3, absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation in the stratosphere?
options: Ozone
Dioxygen
Peroxide
Superoxide
questions.correct_answer: Ozone
questions.explanation: Ozone (O3), a triatomic allotrope of oxygen, forms a protective layer in the stratosphere that absorbs much of the sun's harmful UV-B and UV-C radiation.

questions.question: Which noble gas (Group 18) was among the first to be shown capable of forming chemical compounds, such as XePtF6 and XeF4?
options: Xenon
Helium
Neon
Argon
questions.correct_answer: Xenon
questions.explanation: Xenon's relatively low ionization energy among the noble gases allows it to form genuine chemical compounds with highly electronegative elements like fluorine and oxygen, unlike the lighter, more inert noble gases.

questions.question: Why are noble gases (Group 18) generally chemically unreactive?
options: They possess a complete outer electron shell, giving them a stable electron configuration
They have no electrons in their outer shell at all
They are always found as liquids at room temperature
They react instantly with all other elements
questions.correct_answer: They possess a complete outer electron shell, giving them a stable electron configuration
questions.explanation: Noble gases have a full valence shell (ns2np6, except helium which has 1s2), making them energetically stable and generally unreactive under normal conditions.

questions.question: What is a radioactive isotope (radioisotope)?
options: An unstable form of an element that spontaneously emits radiation as it decays into a more stable nucleus
Any isotope with an even number of neutrons
An isotope that has an identical mass number to its element's most common form
An isotope that cannot undergo any nuclear change
questions.correct_answer: An unstable form of an element that spontaneously emits radiation as it decays into a more stable nucleus
questions.explanation: Radioisotopes have unstable nuclei that spontaneously emit alpha, beta, or gamma radiation as they transform toward a more stable nuclear configuration.

questions.question: During alpha decay, a nucleus emits an alpha particle. What is the composition of an alpha particle?
options: Two protons and two neutrons (equivalent to a helium-4 nucleus)
A single high-energy electron
A single proton only
A photon of electromagnetic radiation
questions.correct_answer: Two protons and two neutrons (equivalent to a helium-4 nucleus)
questions.explanation: An alpha particle is identical to a helium-4 nucleus, consisting of two protons and two neutrons, and its emission decreases the mass number of the parent nucleus by 4 and the atomic number by 2.

questions.question: What happens to the atomic number and mass number of a nucleus that undergoes beta-minus decay (emission of an electron)?
options: The atomic number increases by 1 while the mass number stays the same
The atomic number decreases by 1 while the mass number stays the same
Both the atomic number and mass number decrease by 1
The mass number decreases by 4 and atomic number by 2
questions.correct_answer: The atomic number increases by 1 while the mass number stays the same
questions.explanation: In beta-minus decay, a neutron converts into a proton and an electron; the emitted electron (beta particle) leaves the nucleus, increasing the atomic number by 1 while the mass number remains unchanged since a neutron becomes a proton.

questions.question: What is the term for the time required for half of the atoms in a radioactive sample to decay?
options: Half-life
Decay constant
Mean life
Activity period
questions.correct_answer: Half-life
questions.explanation: Half-life is defined as the time taken for the number of radioactive nuclei in a sample (or its activity) to reduce to half its original value, and it is a constant characteristic of each radioisotope.

questions.question: Which type of nuclear process involves the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei, releasing large amounts of energy, as used in nuclear power plants?
options: Nuclear fission
Nuclear fusion
Radioactive decay only
Electron capture
questions.correct_answer: Nuclear fission
questions.explanation: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus (such as uranium-235) into two smaller nuclei plus neutrons, releasing a large amount of energy, and it is the process harnessed in conventional nuclear power plants.

questions.question: Which oxidation state is most commonly and stably exhibited by iron in its compounds, alongside +3?
options: 0 only
questions.explanation: Iron most commonly exists in the +2 (ferrous) and +3 (ferric) oxidation states in its compounds, reflecting the relative stability of its d6 and d5 electron configurations respectively.

questions.question: Why do transition metals commonly exhibit variable (multiple) oxidation states, unlike most main group metals?
options: The energies of the (n-1)d and ns electrons are similar, so different numbers of electrons can be lost with comparable ease
Transition metals have no valence electrons at all
Transition metals only ever exist as neutral atoms
Transition metals always lose exactly one electron
questions.correct_answer: The energies of the (n-1)d and ns electrons are similar, so different numbers of electrons can be lost with comparable ease
questions.explanation: Because the ns and (n-1)d orbitals are close in energy, transition metals can lose varying numbers of electrons from both subshells without a huge energy penalty, giving rise to their characteristic multiple oxidation states.

questions.question: What structural feature distinguishes a chelate complex, such as that formed between a metal ion and ethylenediamine, from a complex with monodentate ligands?
options: A chelate involves a polydentate ligand forming a ring structure with the metal ion through multiple donor atoms
A chelate complex has no central metal ion
A chelate complex is always negatively charged
A chelate complex can never be more stable than a monodentate complex
questions.correct_answer: A chelate involves a polydentate ligand forming a ring structure with the metal ion through multiple donor atoms
questions.explanation: Chelating ligands like ethylenediamine bond to the metal through two or more donor atoms, forming a ring structure that is generally more thermodynamically stable than an equivalent complex with monodentate ligands, an effect known as the chelate effect.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why transition metals and their compounds are widely used as catalysts?
options: Their variable oxidation states and ability to form complexes allow them to provide alternative reaction pathways
They are always chemically inert and never react with reactants
They have no d electrons available for bonding
They only function as catalysts at extremely low temperatures
questions.correct_answer: Their variable oxidation states and ability to form complexes allow them to provide alternative reaction pathways
questions.explanation: The ability of transition metals to adopt multiple oxidation states and temporarily bond with reactants (forming intermediate complexes) allows them to lower activation energy by providing alternative, lower-energy reaction pathways.

questions.question: According to Bronsted-Lowry theory, water can act as both an acid and a base depending on the reaction. What term describes this dual behaviour?
options: Amphoteric (amphiprotic)
Neutral only
Isoelectronic
Polydentate
questions.correct_answer: Amphoteric (amphiprotic)
questions.explanation: A substance that can act as either a proton donor (acid) or proton acceptor (base) depending on the reaction partner is described as amphoteric (or specifically amphiprotic for proton transfer), as water does in different reactions.

questions.question: Which geometry is most commonly adopted by transition metal complexes with a coordination number of 6, such as [Co(NH3)6]3+?
options: Octahedral
Tetrahedral
Square planar
Linear
questions.correct_answer: Octahedral
questions.explanation: A coordination number of 6 most commonly gives an octahedral geometry, in which six ligands are arranged symmetrically around the central metal ion at 90-degree angles.

questions.question: What is meant by the term 'geometric isomerism' (cis-trans isomerism) in coordination compounds, using [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] as an example?
options: Ligands can be arranged adjacent to each other (cis) or opposite each other (trans) around the metal centre, giving compounds with different properties
The compound has two different central metal atoms
The compound cannot exist in more than one form
Isomerism only occurs when all ligands are identical
questions.correct_answer: Ligands can be arranged adjacent to each other (cis) or opposite each other (trans) around the metal centre, giving compounds with different properties
questions.explanation: In square planar or octahedral complexes with two different types of ligand, the ligands can occupy positions next to each other (cis) or directly across from each other (trans), producing distinct isomers with different physical and chemical properties, as famously seen in cisplatin versus transplatin.

questions.question: Which particle has no charge and no mass number change effect when comparing beta and gamma emissions, being pure electromagnetic radiation rather than a particle?
options: Gamma ray
Alpha particle
Beta particle
Neutron
questions.correct_answer: Gamma ray
questions.explanation: Gamma radiation is high-energy electromagnetic radiation with no mass and no charge; its emission does not change the atomic number or mass number of the nucleus, but it does release energy, often accompanying alpha or beta decay.
